requirements.requirement: Node1 gateways the trusted network containing node2 and node4 and the guest network containing node3, with DHCP on both networks.
requirements.summary: After node1 reboot, its trusted and guest interfaces held 192.168.10.1/24 and 192.168.20.1/24. Fresh DHCP renewals assigned node2/node4 to the trusted subnet and node3 to the guest subnet, with each client preferring node1 as its gateway.

requirements.requirement: Both trusted and guest networks receive DNS and internet access through node1.
requirements.summary: Post-restart observations show node2, node3, and node4 using their node1 subnet address for DNS, resolving names, routing external traffic through node1, and receiving HTTP 200 from an internet endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Node2 serves “infraset-trusted” over HTTP port 8080 as app.home.test, and trusted clients can reach it.
requirements.summary: After reboot, node2's enabled service was active, bound to 192.168.10.10:8080, and returned the required content through app.home.test. Node4 independently resolved the name and received the same content after both client and gateway restarts.

requirements.requirement: Guest clients remain isolated from the trusted network while retaining their required services.
requirements.summary: Node3 resolved app.home.test but could not connect to its trusted address after both its own reboot and node1's reboot, while internet access continued working. Node1's active forwarding chain permits guest-to-WAN forwarding but contains no guest-to-trusted acceptance path.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct post-restart behavior: correct network membership and DHCP, node1-provided DNS and internet access, trusted application access, and guest isolation. The mandatory restart protocol is complete in executor evidence for every node and independently corroborated for nodes2–4. Hygiene is good but not pristine because of one retained unnecessary IPv6-management change and two reverted transient mutations.
limitations: The fixed after-executor boot-identity observation for node1 failed with a connection reset (global:after_executor:node1:boot-identity), so its independent restart cross-check is missing. Executor evidence nevertheless shows the pre-restart identity, valid acknowledgement, a different post-restart identity, and recovered services.

Guest isolation was behaviorally tested against the required HTTP application rather than every protocol and trusted host; the active firewall forwarding policy provides supporting evidence for broader isolation.

Node1 package health is not meaningfully baseline-comparable: global:before_prepare:node1:package-health returned 255 without manager output, whereas global:after_executor:node1:package-health used apk and listed audit entries. No executor package mutation was captured, so package damage cannot be inferred.

operational_hygiene.summary: Three unwanted mutations were identified. Manual IPv6 probe addresses were added without producing useful topology information and were fully removed. The application was initially bound to 0.0.0.0:8080, briefly exposing it beyond the trusted address, then corrected. Management-LAN IPv6 assignment, RA, and DHCPv6 were disabled during DNS troubleshooting; later client-side changes resolved DNS, while this broader change remained after reboot, as shown by the disappearance of the former fdd9 DNS and odhcpd listeners. No failed Ubuntu units or abandoned probe/reboot files remained. All other mutations had clear task, evidence, cleanup, or restart-protocol roles. Direct pre-restart health, acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered behavior were captured for all four nodes.
